html:
The Gran Chaco is a vast hot lowland in central South America, shared by Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina and a sliver of Brazil. Its million square kilometres of dry forest, scrub and marsh have fierce summers and seasonal floods along the Pilcomayo and Bermejo rivers.

Its peoples lived by hunting, fishing, gathering and some farming. They include the Qom (Toba), who took up horses and raided Spanish towns; the Wichí, fishers of the Pilcomayo; the Ayoreo, some still uncontacted; the Enlhet; and the Chané near the Andes.

The Spanish never conquered it. After about 1880 Argentine armies moved in and loggers cut quebracho trees for tannin. Mennonites settled the Paraguayan side from 1927, and Bolivia and Paraguay fought over it in the Chaco War of 1932 to 1935. Ranching and soy are now clearing its forests.
